entries.71757825d08c5396a7a278449ff9855be1f31cf3: <div sID="gen13046" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="132" osisID="Ps.132" sID="Ps.132"/> <div eID="gen13046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13047" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13048" type="x-p"/> It is probable that this psalm was penned by Solomon, to be sung at the dedication of the temple which he built according to the charge his father gave him, <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.2-1Chr.28.21">1 Chron. xxviii. 2</reference>, &c. Having fulfilled his trust, he begs of God to own what he had done. I. He had built this house for the honour and service of God; and when he brings the ark into it, the token of God's presence, he desires that God himself would come and take possession of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.8-Ps.132.10">ver. 8-10</reference>. With these words Solomon concluded his prayer, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.41-2Chr.6.42">2 Chron. vi. 41, 42</reference>. II. He had built it in pursuance of the orders he had received from his father, and therefore his pleas to enforce these petitions refer to David. 1. He pleads David's piety towards God, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.1-Ps.132.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. 2. He pleads God's promise to David, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.11-Ps.132.18">ver. 11-18</reference>. The former introduces his petition: the latter follows it as an answer to it. In singing this psalm we must have a concern for the gospel church as the temple of God, and a dependence upon Christ as David our King, in whom the mercies of God are sure mercies.
entries.e2b74237152520d37cd182e506b23c6c6537f721: <div eID="gen13048" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13047" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Solomon's Prayer for Divine Favour.</title> <div sID="gen13049" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , remember David, <hi type="italic">and</hi> all his afflictions: <hi type="super">2</hi> How he sware unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">and</hi> vowed unto the mighty <hi type="italic">God</hi> of Jacob; <hi type="super">3</hi> Surely I will not come into the tabernacle of my house, nor go up into my bed; <hi type="super">4</hi> I will not give sleep to mine eyes, <hi type="italic">or</hi> slumber to mine eyelids, 5 Until I find out a place for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , a habitation for the mighty <hi type="italic">God</hi> of Jacob. <hi type="super">6</hi> Lo, we heard of it at Ephratah: we found it in the fields of the wood. <hi type="super">7</hi> We will go into his tabernacles: we will worship at his footstool. <hi type="super">8</hi> Arise, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , into thy rest; thou, and the ark of thy strength. <hi type="super">9</hi> Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness; and let thy saints shout for joy. <hi type="super">10</hi> For thy servant David's sake turn not away the face of thine anointed. <div eID="gen13049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13050" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have Solomon's address to God for his favour to him and to his government, and his acceptance of his building a house to God's name. Observe, <div eID="gen13050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13051" type="x-p"/> I. What he pleads—two things:— <div eID="gen13051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13052" type="x-p"/> 1. That what he had done was in pursuance of the pious vow which his father David had made to build a house for God. Solomon was a wise man, yet pleads not any merit of his own: "I am not worthy, for whom thou shouldst do this; but, <hi type="italic">Lord, remember David,</hi> with whom thou madest the covenant" (as Moses prayed, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.13">Exod. xxxii. 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">Remember Abraham,</hi> the first trustee of the covenant); "remember <hi type="italic">all his afflictions,</hi> all the troubles of his life, which his being anointed was the occasion of," or his care and concern about the ark, and what an uneasiness it was to him that the ark was in curtains, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.2">2 Sam. vii. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Remember all his humility and meekness</hi> (so some read it), all that pious and devout affection with which he had made the following vow. Note, It is not amiss for us to put God in mind of our predecessors in profession, of their afflictions, their services, and their sufferings, of God's covenant with them, the experiences they have had of his goodness, the care they took of, and the many prayers they put up for, those that should come after them. We may apply it to Christ, the Son of David, and to all his afflictions: "Lord, remember the covenant made with him and the satisfaction made by him. <hi type="italic">Remember all his offerings</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.3">Ps. xx. 3</reference>), that is, all his sufferings." He especially pleads the solemn vow that David had made as soon as ever he was settled in his government, and before he was well settled in a house of his own, that he would build a house for God. Observe, (1.) Whom he bound himself to, <hi type="italic">to the Lord, to the mighty God of Jacob.</hi> Vows are to be made to God, who is a party as well as a witness. The Lord is the Mighty One of Jacob, Jacob's God, and a mighty one, whose power is engaged for Jacob's defence and deliverance. Jacob is weak, but the God of Jacob is a mighty one. (2.) What he bound himself to do, to <hi type="italic">find out a place for the Lord,</hi> that is, for the ark, the token of his presence. He had observed in the law frequent mention of the <hi type="italic">place that God would choose to put his name there,</hi> to which all the tribes should resort. When he came to the crown there was no such place; Shiloh was deserted, and no other place was pitched upon, for want of which the feasts of the Lord were not kept with due solemnity. "Well," says David, "I will find out such a place for the general rendezvous of all the tribes, a place of <hi type="italic">habitation for the Mighty</hi> One <hi type="italic">of Jacob,</hi> a place for the ark, where there shall be room both for the priests and people to attend upon it." (3.) How intent he was upon it; he would not settle in his bed, till he had brought this matter to some head, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.3-Ps.132.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. The thing had been long talked of, and nothing done, till at last David, when he went out one morning about public business, made a vow that before night he would come to a resolution in this matter, and would determine the place either where the tent should be pitched for the reception of the ark, at the beginning of his reign, or rather where Solomon should build the temple, which was not fixed till the latter end of his reign, just after the pestilence with which he was punished for numbering the people (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.1">1 Chron. xxii. 1</reference>, <hi type="italic">Then David said, This is the house of the Lord</hi>); and perhaps it was upon occasion of that judgment that he made this vow, being apprehensive that one of God's controversies with him was for his dilatoriness in this matter. Note, When needful work is to be done for God it is good for us to task ourselves, and tie ourselves to a time, because we are apt to put off. It is good in the morning to cut out work for the day, binding ourselves that we will do it before we sleep, only with submission to Providence; for we <hi type="italic">know not what a day may bring forth.</hi> Especially in the great work of conversion to God we must be thus solicitous, thus zealous; we have good reason to resolve that we will not enjoy the comforts of this life till we have laid a foundation for hopes of a better. <div eID="gen13052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13053" type="x-p"/> 2. That it was in pursuance of the expectations of the people of Israel, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.6-Ps.132.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. (1.) They were inquisitive after the ark; for they lamented its obscurity, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.2">1 Sam. vii. 2</reference>. They <hi type="italic">heard of it at Ephratah</hi> (that is, at Shiloh, in the tribe of Ephraim); there they were told it had been, but it was gone. They <hi type="italic">found it,</hi> at last, <hi type="italic">in the fields of the wood,</hi> that is, in Kirjath-jearim, which signifies <hi type="italic">the city of woods.</hi> Thence all Israel fetched it, with great solemnity, in the beginning of David's reign (<reference osisRef="1Chr.13.6">1 Chron. xiii. 6</reference>), so that in building his house for the ark Solomon had gratified all Israel. They needed not to go about to seek the ark anymore; they now knew where to find it. (2.) They were resolved to attend it: "Let us but have a convenient place, and <hi type="italic">we will go into his tabernacle,</hi> to pay our homage there; <hi type="italic">we will worship at his footstool</hi> as subjects and suppliants, which we neglected to do, for want of such a place, <hi type="italic">in the days of Saul,</hi>" <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.3">1 Chron. xiii. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen13053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13054" type="x-p"/> II. What he prays for, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.8-Ps.132.10">v. 8-10</reference>. 1. That God would vouchsafe, not only to take possession of, but to take up his residence in, this temple which he had built: <hi type="italic">Arise, O Lord! into thy rest,</hi> and let this be it, <hi type="italic">thou,</hi> even <hi type="italic">the ark of thy strength,</hi> the pledge of thy presence, thy mighty presence. 2. That God would give grace to the ministers of the sanctuary to do their duty: <hi type="italic">Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness;</hi> let them appear righteous both in their administrations and in their conversations, and let both be according to the rule. Note, Righteousness is the best ornament of a minister. Holiness towards God, and goodness towards all men, are habits for ministers of the necessity of which there is no dispute. "They are <hi type="italic">thy priests,</hi> and will therefore discredit their relation to thee if they <hi type="italic">be not clothed with righteousness.</hi>" 3. That the people of God might have the comfort of the due administration of holy ordinances among them: <hi type="italic">Let thy saints shout for joy.</hi> They did so when the ark was brought into the city of David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.15">2 Sam. vi. 15</reference>); they will do so when the priests are clothed with righteousness. A faithful ministry is the joy of the saints; it is the matter of it; it is a friend and a furtherance to it; we are <hi type="italic">helpers of your joy,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.24">2 Cor. i. 24</reference>. 4. That Solomon's own prayer, upon occasion of the dedicating of the temple, might be accepted of God: "<hi type="italic">Turn not away the face of thy anointed,</hi> that is, deny me not the things I have asked of thee, send me not away ashamed." He pleads, (1.) That he was the anointed of the Lord, and this he pleads as a type of Christ, the great anointed, who, in his intercession, urges his designation to his office. He is God's anointed, and therefore the Father hears him always. (2.) That he was the son of David: "For his sake do not deny me;" and this is the Christian's plea: "For the sake of Christ" (our David), "<hi type="italic">in whom thou art well pleased,</hi> accept me." He is David, whose name signifies <hi type="italic">beloved;</hi> and we are made accepted in the beloved. He is God's servant, whom he <hi type="italic">upholds,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa. xlii. 1</reference>. "We have no merit of our own to plead, but for his sake, in whom there is a fulness of merit, let us find favour." When we pray for the prosperity of the church we may pray with great boldness, for Christ's sake, who purchased the church with his own blood. "Let both ministers and people do their duty."
entries.63c4f99c13dd9ed401a0b9c13adf5e2b572e0586: <div eID="gen13054" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Choice of Zion; God's Promises to Zion.</title> <div sID="gen13055" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath sworn <hi type="italic">in</hi> truth unto David; he will not turn from it; Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne. <hi type="super">12</hi> If thy children will keep my covenant and my testimony that I shall teach them, their children shall also sit upon thy throne for evermore. 13 For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath chosen Zion; he hath desired <hi type="italic">it</hi> for his habitation. <hi type="super">14</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> my rest for ever: here will I dwell; for I have desired it. <hi type="super">15</hi> I will abundantly bless her provision: I will satisfy her poor with bread. <hi type="super">16</hi> I will also clothe her priests with salvation: and her saints shall shout aloud for joy. <hi type="super">17</hi> There will I make the horn of David to bud: I have ordained a lamp for mine anointed. <hi type="super">18</hi> His enemies will I clothe with shame: but upon himself shall his crown flourish. <div eID="gen13055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13056" type="x-p"/> These are precious promises, <hi type="italic">confirmed by an oath,</hi> that the heirs of them might have <hi type="italic">strong consolation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.17-Heb.6.18">Heb. vi. 17, 18</reference>. It is all one whether we take them as pleas urged in the prayer or as answers returned to the prayer; believers know how to make use of the promises both ways, with them to speak to God and in them to hear what God the Lord will speak to us. These promises relate to the establishment both in church and state, both to the throne of the house of David and to the testimony of Israel fixed on Mount Zion. The promises concerning Zion's hill are as applicable to the gospel-church as these concerning David's seed are to Christ, and therefore both pleadable by us and very comfortable to us. Here is, <div eID="gen13056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13057" type="x-p"/> I. The choice God made of David's house and Zion hill. Both were of divine appointment. <div eID="gen13057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13058" type="x-p"/> 1. God chose David's family for the royal family and confirmed his choice by an oath, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.11-Ps.132.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. David, being a type of Christ, was made king with an oath: <hi type="italic">The Lord hath sworn and will not repent,</hi> will not turn from it. Did David swear to the Lord (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.2">v. 2</reference>) that he would find him a house? The Lord swore to David that he would build him a house; for God will be behind with none of his people in affections or assurances. The promise made to David refers, (1.) To a long succession of kings that should descend from his loins: <hi type="italic">Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne,</hi> which was fulfilled in Solomon; David himself lived to see it with great satisfaction, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.48">1 Kings i. 48</reference>. The crown was also entailed conditionally upon his heirs for ever: <hi type="italic">If thy children,</hi> in following ages, <hi type="italic">will keep my covenant and my testimony that I shall teach them.</hi> God himself engaged to teach them, and he did his part; they had Moses and the prophets, and all he expects is that they should keep what he taught them, and keep to it, and then <hi type="italic">their children shall sit upon thy throne for evermore.</hi> Kings are before God upon their good behaviour, and their commission from him runs <hi type="italic">quamdiu se bene gesserint—during good behaviour.</hi> The issue of this was that they did not keep God's covenant, and so the entail was at length cut off, and <hi type="italic">the sceptre departed from Judah</hi> by degrees. (2.) To an everlasting successor, a king that should descend from his loins of <hi type="italic">the increase of whose government and peace there shall be no end.</hi> St. Peter applies this to Christ, nay, he tells us that David himself so understood it. <reference osisRef="Acts.2.30">Acts ii. 30</reference>, <hi type="italic">He knew that God had sworn with an oath to him that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne;</hi> and in the fulness of time he did so, and <hi type="italic">gave him the throne of his father David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.32">Luke i. 32</reference>. He did fulfill the condition of the promise; he kept God's covenant and his testimony, did his Father's will, and in all things pleased him; and therefore to him, and his spiritual seed, the promise shall be made good. He, and the children God has given him, all believers, shall <hi type="italic">sit upon the throne for evermore,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Rev. iii. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen13058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13059" type="x-p"/> 2. God chose Zion hill for the holy hill, and confirmed his choice by the delight he took in it, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.13-Ps.132.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. He <hi type="italic">chose the Mount Zion which he loved</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.68">Ps. lxxviii. 68</reference>); he chose it for the habitation of his ark, and said of it, <hi type="italic">This is my rest for ever,</hi> and not merely my residence for a time, as Shiloh was. Zion was the city of David; he chose it for the royal city because God chose it for the holy city. God said, <hi type="italic">Here will I dwell,</hi> and therefore David said, <hi type="italic">Here will I dwell,</hi> for here he adhered to his principle, <hi type="italic">It is good for me to be near to God.</hi> Zion must be here looked upon as a type of the gospel-church, which is called <hi type="italic">Mount Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">Heb. xii. 22</reference>), and in it what is here said of Zion has its full accomplishment. Zion was long since ploughed as a field, but the church of Christ <hi type="italic">is the house of the living God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">1 Tim. iii. 15</reference>), and it is his <hi type="italic">rest for ever,</hi> and shall be blessed with his presence always, even to the end of the world. The delight God takes in his church, and the continuance of his presence with his church, are the comfort and joy of all its members. <div eID="gen13059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13060" type="x-p"/> II. The choice blessings God has in store for David's house and Zion hill. Whom God chooses he will bless. <div eID="gen13060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13061" type="x-p"/> 1. God, having chosen Zion hill, promises to bless that, <div eID="gen13061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13062" type="x-p"/> (1.) With the blessings of the life that now is; for godliness has the promise of them, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.15">v. 15</reference>. The earth shall yield her increase; where religion is set up there shall be provision, and in blessing God will bless it (<reference osisRef="Ps.67.6">Ps. lxvii. 6</reference>); he will surely and abundantly bless it. And a little provision, with an abundant blessing upon it, will be more serviceable, as well as more comfortable, than a great deal without that blessing. God's people have a special blessing upon common enjoyments, and that blessing puts a peculiar sweetness into them. Nay, the promise goes further: <hi type="italic">I will satisfy her poor with bread.</hi> Zion has her own poor to keep; and it is promised that God will take care even of them. [1.] By his providence they shall be kept from wanting; they shall have provision enough. If there be scarcity, the poor are the first that feel it, so that it is a sure sign of plenty if they have sufficient. Zion's poor shall not want, for God has obliged all the sons of Zion to be charitable to the poor, according to their ability, and the church must take care that they be not <hi type="italic">neglected,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.6.1">Acts vi. 1</reference>. [2.] By his grace they shall be kept from complaining; though they have but dry bread, yet they shall be satisfied. Zion's poor have, of all others, reason to be content with a little of this world, because they have better things prepared for them. And this may be understood spiritually of the provision that is made for the soul in the word and ordinances; God will abundantly bless that for the nourishment of the new man, and satisfy the poor in spirit with the bread of life. What God sanctifies to us we shall and may be satisfied with. <div eID="gen13062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13063" type="x-p"/> (2.) With the blessings of the life that is to come, things pertaining to godliness (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.16">v. 16</reference>), which is an answer to the prayer, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.9">v. 9</reference>. [1.] It was desired that the priests might be <hi type="italic">clothed with righteousness;</hi> it is here promised that God will <hi type="italic">clothe them with salvation,</hi> not only save them, but make them and their administrations instrumental for the salvation of his people; they shall both <hi type="italic">save themselves and those that hear them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">add those to the church that shall be saved.</hi> Note, Whom God clothes with righteousness he will clothe with salvation; we must pray for righteousness and then with it God will give salvation. [2.] It was desired that the saints might <hi type="italic">shout for joy;</hi> it is promised that they <hi type="italic">shall shout aloud for joy.</hi> God gives more than we ask, and when he gives salvation he will give an abundant joy. <div eID="gen13063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13064" type="x-p"/> 2. God, having chosen David's family, here promises to bless that also with suitable blessings. (1.) Growing power: <hi type="italic">There,</hi> in Zion, <hi type="italic">will I make the horn of David to bud,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.132.17">v. 17</reference>. The royal dignity shall increase more and more, and constant additions he made to the lustre of it. Christ is the <hi type="italic">horn of salvation</hi> (denoting a plentiful and powerful salvation) which God has raised up, and made to bud, <hi type="italic">in the house of his servant David.</hi> David had promised to use his power for God's glory, to cut off the horns of the wicked, and to exalt the horns of the righteous (<reference osisRef="Ps.75.10">Ps. lxxv. 10</reference>); in recompence for it God here promises to make his horn to bud, for to those that have power, and use it well, more shall be given. (2.) Lasting honour: <hi type="italic">I have ordained a lamp for my anointed.</hi> Thou wilt <hi type="italic">light my candle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.28">Ps. xviii. 28</reference>. That lamp is likely to burn brightly which God ordains. A lamp is a successor, for, when a lamp is almost out, another may be lighted by it; it is a succession, for by this means David shall not want a man to stand before God. Christ is the lamp and the light of the world. (3.) Complete victory: "<hi type="italic">His enemies,</hi> who have formed designs against him, <hi type="italic">will I clothe with shame,</hi> when they shall see their designs baffled." Let the enemies of all good governors expect to be clothed with shame, and especially the enemies of the Lord Jesus and his government, who shall rise, in the great day, <hi type="italic">to everlasting shame and contempt.</hi> (4.) Universal prosperity: <hi type="italic">Upon himself shall his crown flourish,</hi> that is, his government shall be more and more his honour. This was to have its full accomplishment in Jesus Christ, whose crown of honour and power shall never fade, nor the flowers of it wither. The crowns of earthly princes <hi type="italic">endure not to all generations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.24">Prov. xxvii. 24</reference>), but Christ's crown shall endure to all eternity and the crowns reserved for his faithful subjects are such as <hi type="italic">fade not away.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.132"/> <div eID="gen13064" type="x-p"/>

entries.d39e8f181dc51ae33fd832c72601ea169ada7f76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7039"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 132</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.132.1-Ps.132.18">Psa 132:1-18</reference>. The writer, perhaps Solomon (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.132.8">Psa 132:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.9">9</reference>), after relating David's pious zeal for God's service, pleads for the fulfilment of the promise (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.16">2Sa 7:16</reference>), which, providing for a perpetuation of David's kingdom, involved that of God's right worship and the establishment of the greater and spiritual kingdom of David's greater Son. Of Him and His kingdom both the temple and its worship, and the kings and kingdom of Judah, were types. The congruity of such a topic with the tenor of this series of Psalms is obvious.</title> <div sID="gen10799" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7039"/>1-5. This vow is not elsewhere recorded. It expresses, in strong language, David's intense desire to see the establishment of God's worship as well as of His kingdom.<div eID="gen10799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10800" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remember David--</hi>literally, "remember for David," that is, all his troubles and anxieties on the matter. <div eID="gen10800" type="x-p"/>
entries.660d5ef0a97f7e382ce880431169bbec9287c0b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7041"/><div sID="gen10802" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7041"/>6. These may be the "words of David" and his pious friends, who,<div eID="gen10802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10803" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at Ephratah--</hi>or Beth-lehem (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.7">Ge 48:7</reference>), where he once lived, may have heard of the ark, which he found for the first time<div eID="gen10803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the fields of the wood--</hi>or, Jair, or Kirjath-jearim ("City of woods") (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.1">1Sa 7:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.3">2Sa 6:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.4">4</reference>), whence it was brought to Zion. <div eID="gen10804" type="x-p"/>
entries.3434ad9bf7aa5dfdc4e74c8ac6677ccbcac11138: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7042"/><div sID="gen10805" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7042"/>7. The purpose of engaging in God's worship is avowed. <div eID="gen10805" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf87ba502f4b4ed802b0ee869a137a840170a423: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7043"/><div sID="gen10806" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7043"/>8-9. The solemn entry of the ark, symbolical of God's presence and power, with the attending priests, into the sanctuary, is proclaimed in the words used by Solomon (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.41">2Ch 6:41</reference>). <div eID="gen10806" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca6e3ac30bd24468a0e7e90c0769aabfde735557: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7044"/><div sID="gen10807" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7044"/><hi type="bold">10-12. For thy servant David's sake--</hi>that is, On account of the promise made to him.<div eID="gen10807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10808" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turn ... anointed--</hi>Repulse not him who, as David's descendant, pleads the promise to perpetuate his royal line. After reciting the promise, substantially from <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.12-2Sam.7.16">2Sa 7:12-16</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.2.30">Ac 2:30</reference>, &c.), an additional plea, <div eID="gen10808" type="x-p"/>
entries.d183281c79a125f423b7bb312aaeebefb9c9ccad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7045"/><div sID="gen10809" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7045"/>13. is made on the ground of God's choice of Zion (here used for Jerusalem) as His dwelling, inasmuch as the prosperity of the kingdom was connected with that of the Church (<reference osisRef="Ps.122.8">Psa 122:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.122.9">9</reference>). <div eID="gen10809" type="x-p"/>
entries.2585a2d72b3e4b91e82995dbffb9c06c8f2f69c7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7046"/><div sID="gen10810" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7046"/>14-18. That choice is expressed in God's words, "I will sit" or "dwell," or sit enthroned. The joy of the people springs from the blessings of His grace, conferred through the medium of the priesthood. <div eID="gen10810" type="x-p"/>

entries.0bdaf940705bc4be9e9af1dd7732067fe94ec8fb: <div eID="gen23175" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23176" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23177" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23177" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23176" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23178" type="x-p"/> The psalmist prays that God would remember his promises to David, <reference osisRef="Psa.132.1">Psa 132:1</reference>. His purpose to bring the ark of the Lord into a place of rest, <reference osisRef="Psa.132.2-Psa.132.5">Psa 132:2-5</reference>. Where it was found, and the prayer in removing it, <reference osisRef="Psa.132.6-Psa.132.9">Psa 132:6-9</reference>. The promises made to David and his posterity, <reference osisRef="Psa.132.10-Psa.132.12">Psa 132:10-12</reference>. God's choice of Zion for a habitation, and his promises to the people, <reference osisRef="Psa.132.13-Psa.132.17">Psa 132:13-17</reference>. All their enemies shall be confounded, <reference osisRef="Psa.132.18">Psa 132:18</reference>. <div eID="gen23178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23179" type="x-p"/> Some attribute this Psalm to David, but without sufficient ground; others, to Solomon, with more likelihood; and others, to some inspired author at the conclusion of the captivity, which is, perhaps, the most probable. It refers to the building of the second temple, and placing the ark of the covenant in it. <div eID="gen23179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23180" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23181" type="x-p"/> Lord, remember David - Consider the promises thou hast made to this thy eminent servant, that had respect, not only to him and to his family, but to all the Israelitish people.
entries.4f281d2fdf39b372cfcff39b1854ff016553de15: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23182" type="x-p"/> How he sware unto the Lord - It is only in this place that we are informed of David's vow to the Lord, relative to the building of the temple; but we find he had fully purposed the thing.
entries.b28167bb740d132a0e88928e0e05ba4063f871c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23183" type="x-p"/> Surely I will not come - This must refer to the situation of the temple; or, as we would express it, he would not pass another day till he had found out the ground on which to build the temple, and projected the plan, and devised ways and means to execute it. And we find that he would have acted in all things according to his oath and vow, had God permitted him. But even after the Lord told him that Solomon, not he, should build the house he still continued to show his good will by collecting treasure and materials for the building, all the rest of his life.
entries.890c7fdf0cdcc83f7f5090e2bf23dbcc9497958e: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23184" type="x-p"/> The mighty God of Jacob - עביר יעקב abir yaacob, the Mighty One of Jacob. We have this epithet of God for the first time, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.24">Gen 49:24</reference>. Hence, perhaps, the abirim of the heathen, the stout ones, the strong beings.
entries.3acb580ab7d7ff98a3376ffd9c1b27f3a62abcf2: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23185" type="x-p"/> Lo, we have heard of it at Ephratah - This may be considered as a continuation of David's vow, as if he had said: As I had determined to build a temple for the ark, and heard that it was at Ephratah, I went and found it in the fields of Jaar, יער; - not the wood, but Kirjath Jaar or Jearim, where the ark was then lodged; - and having found it, he entered the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Psa.132.7">Psa 132:7</reference>; and then, adoring that God whose presence was in it, he invited him to arise and come to the place which he had prepared for him.
entries.89f9e520673e201847cb76a52b6b352f17b6f812: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23186" type="x-p"/> Arise, O Lord, into thy rest; thou and the ark of thy strength - Using the same expressions which Solomon used when he dedicated the temple, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.41">2Chr 6:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.42">2Chr 6:42</reference>. There are several difficulties in these passages. Ephratah may mean the tribe of Ephraim; and then we may understand the place thus: "I have learned that the ark had been in the tribe of Ephraim, and I have seen it at Kirjath-jearim, or Field of the woods, but this is not a proper place for it, for the Lord hath chosen Jerusalem." It is true that the ark did remain in that tribe from the days of Joshua to Samuel, during three hundred and twenty-eight years; and thence it was brought to Kirjath-jearim, where it continued seventy years, till the commencement of the reign of David over all Israel. <div eID="gen23186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23187" type="x-p"/> But if we take <reference osisRef="Psa.132.6-Psa.132.8">Psa 132:6-8</reference>, not as the continuation of David's vow, but as the words of the captives in Babylon, the explanation will be more plain and easy: "We have heard, O Lord, from our fathers, that thy tabernacle was formerly a long time at Shiloh, in the tribe of Ephraim. And our history informs us that it has been also at Kirjath-jearim, the fields of the wood; and afterwards it was brought to Jerusalem, and there established: but Jerusalem is now ruined, the temple destroyed, and thy people in captivity. Arise, O Lord, and reestablish thy dwelling-place in thy holy city!" See Calmet and others on this place.
entries.0eb4c8d5cd2de66c1d8ed58d495cf0e3b9899ccd: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen23187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23188" type="x-p"/> Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness - Let them be as remarkable for inward holiness as they are for the splendor of their holy vestments.
entries.1868479c8337c591b6fd55048a5431aa2b5d81ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen23188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23189" type="x-p"/> The face of thine anointed - David. Remember thy promises to him, that he may be restored to thee and to thy worship.
entries.c015d3268d5bbccbbe8033677cc5973f23ca8e29: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen23189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23190" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath sworn - As David sware to the Lord, so the Lord swears to David that he will establish his throne, and place his posterity on it: and that he had respect to David's Antitype, we learn from St. Peter, <reference osisRef="Act.2.30">Act 2:30</reference> (note), where see the note. This verse with the following refers to the spiritual David, and the Christian Church.
entries.7696659e6bbba04716953ac7f71c8b4f9b51b973: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen23190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23191" type="x-p"/> If thy children will keep my covenant - This was conditional with respect to the posterity of David. They have been driven from the throne, because they did not keep the Lord's covenant, but the true David is on the throne, and his posterity forms the genuine Israelites.
entries.fa23c6f655a4cabb35f44237e7d00a8baa85f87a: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen23191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23192" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath chosen Zion - Therefore neither Shiloh nor Kirjath-jearim is the place of his rest.
entries.c4a33e3c9cf8a1cb79292773f6c80550a8d2c65e: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen23192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23193" type="x-p"/> This is my rest for ever - Here the Christian Church is most indubitably meant. This is God's place for ever. After this there never will be another dispensation; Christianity closes and completes all communications from heaven to earth. God has nothing greater to give to mankind on this side heaven; nor does man need any thing better; nor is his nature capable of any thing more excellent.
entries.2cd846a3bfd79c7f70ec4e78bd53d66764ce4ca2: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen23193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23194" type="x-p"/> I will abundantly bless her provision - There shall be an abundant provision of salvation made for mankind in the Christian Church. Our Lord's multiplication of the loaves was a type and proof of it.
entries.00382160b552166a9ad348f666d7e1adda213e2c: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen23194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23195" type="x-p"/> I will also clothe her priests - All Christian ministers, with salvation; this shall appear in all their conduct. Salvation - redemption from all sin through the blood of the Lamb shall be their great and universal message.
entries.9feec21e7492d7c16a0c55b4d01b4b02ddce4b74: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen23195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23196" type="x-p"/> There will I make the horn of David to bud - There, in the Christian Church, the power and authority of the spiritual David shall appear. <div eID="gen23196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23197" type="x-p"/> I have ordained a lamp - I have taken care to secure a posterity, to which the promises shall be expressly fulfilled.
entries.5ac1ce75f9b926b52e96492399dc3466963c47f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen23197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23198" type="x-p"/> His enemies will I clothe with shame - Every opponent of the Christian cause shall be confounded. <div eID="gen23198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23199" type="x-p"/> But upon himself shall his crown flourish - There shall be no end of the government of Christ's kingdom. From <reference osisRef="Psa.132.11-Psa.132.18">Psa 132:11-18</reference>, the spiritual David and his posterity are the subjects of which the Psalm treats.  <chapter eID="Ps.132"/> <div eID="gen23199" type="x-p"/>

entries.3b7a69077b81652a53e1642da4a487b96777d277: <div eID="gen10223" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Prayer for the House of God and the House of David</title> <div sID="gen10224" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.131.1-Ps.131.3">Psa 131:1-3</reference> designedly precedes Psalms 132. The former has grown out of the memory of an utterance of David when he brought home the Ark, and the latter begins with the remembrance of David’s humbly zealous endeavour to obtain a settled and worthy abode for the God who sits enthroned above the Ark among His people. It is the only Psalm in which the sacred Ark is mentioned. The chronicler put <reference osisRef="Ps.132.8-Ps.132.10">Psa 132:8-10</reference> into the mouth of Solomon at the dedication of the Temple (2Ch 6:41.). After a passage borrowed from <reference osisRef="Ps.130.2">Psa 130:2</reference> which is attached by עתּה to Solomon’s Temple-dedication prayer, he appends further borrowed passages out of Psalms 132 with ועתּה. The variations in these verses of the Psalms, which are annexed by him with a free hand and from memory (<hi type="italic">Jahve Elohim for Jahve</hi>, לנוּחך for למנוּחתך, תּשׁוּעה for צדק, בּטּוב ישׂמחוּ for ירנּנוּ), just as much prove that he has altered the Psalm, and not reversely (as Hitzig persistently maintains), that the psalmist has borrowed from the Chronicles. It is even still distinctly to be seen how the memory of <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Isa 55:3</reference> has influenced the close of <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.42">2Ch 6:42</reference> in the chronicler, just as the memory of <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Isa 55:2</reference> has perhaps also influenced the close of 2Ch 6:41. <div eID="gen10224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10225" type="x-p"/> The psalmist supplicates the divine favour for the anointed of Jahve for David’s sake. In this connection this anointed one is neither the high priest, nor Israel, which is never so named (vid., <reference osisRef="Hab.3.13">Hab 3:13</reference>), nor David himself, who “in all the necessities of his race and people stands before God,” as Hengstenberg asserts, in order to be able to assign this Son of degrees, as others, likewise to the post-exilic time of the new colony. Zerubbabel might more readily be understood (Baur), with whom, according to the closing prophecy of the Book of Haggai, a new period of the Davidic dominion is said to begin. But even Zerubbabel, the פּחת יהוּדה, could not be called משׁיח, for this he was not. The chronicler applies the Psalm in accordance with its contents. It is suited to the mouth of Solomon. The view that it was composed by Solomon himself when the Ark of the covenant was removed out of the tent-temple on Zion into the Temple-building (Amyraldus, De Wette, Tholuck, and others), is favoured by the relation of the circumstances, as they are narrated in 2Ch 5:5., to the desires of the Psalm, and a close kinship of the Psalm with Ps 72 in breadth, repetitions of words, and a laboured forward movement which is here and there a somewhat uncertain advance. At all events it belongs to a time in which the Davidic throne was still standing and the sacred Ark was not as yet irrecoverably lost. That which, according to 2 Sam. 6, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.1">2Sa 7:1</reference>, David did for the glory of Jahve, and on the other hand is promised to him by Jahve, is here made by a post-Davidic poet into the foundation of a hopeful intercessory prayer for the kingship and priesthood of Zion and the church presided over by both. <div eID="gen10225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10226" type="x-p"/> The Psalm consists of four ten-line strophes. Only in connection with the first could any objection be raised, and the strophe be looked upon as only consisting of nine lines. But the other strophes decide the question of its measure; and the breaking up of the weighty <reference osisRef="Ps.132.1">Psa 132:1</reference> into two lines follows the accentuation, which divides it into two parts and places את by itself as being את (according to <hi type="italic">Accentssystem</hi>, xviii. 2, with <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>). Each strophe is adorned once with the name of <hi type="italic">David</hi>; and moreover the step-like progress which comes back to what has been said, and takes up the thread and carries it forward, cannot fail to be recognised.
entries.6e7429ffa88a7d10d9e5c85fa19d109a4730dc37: <reference osisRef="Ps.132.1-Ps.132.5">Psa 132:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen10226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10227" type="x-p"/> One is said to remember anything to another when he requites him something that he has done for him, or when he does for him what he has promised him. It is the post-Davidic church which here reminds Jahve of the hereinafter mentioned promises (of the “mercies of David,” <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.42">2Ch 6:42</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Isa 55:3</reference>) with which He has responded to David’s ענות. By this verbal substantive of the <hi type="italic">Pual</hi> is meant all the care and trouble which David had in order to procure a worthy abode for the sanctuary of Jahve. ענה ב signifies to trouble or harass one’s self about anything, <hi type="italic">afflictari</hi> (as frequently in the Book of Ecclesiastes); the <hi type="italic">Pual</hi> here denotes the self-imposed trouble, or even that imposed by outward circumsntaces, such as the tedious wars, of long, unsuccessful, and yet never relaxed endeavours (1Ki 5:17). For he had vowed unto God that he would give himself absolutely no rest until he had obtained a fixed abode for Jahve. What he said to Nathan (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.2">2Sa 7:2</reference>) is an indication of this vowed resolve, which was now in a time of triumphant peace, as it seemed, ready for being carried out, after the first step towards it had already been taken in the removal of the Ark of the covenant to Zion (2 Sam. 6); ); for 2 Sam 7 is appended to 2 Sam. 6 out of its chronological order and only on account of the internal connection. After the bringing home of the Ark, which had been long yearned for (<reference osisRef="Ps.101.2">Psa 101:2</reference>), and did not take place without difficulties and terrors, was accomplished, a series of years again passed over, during which David always carried about with him the thought of erecting God a Temple-building. And when he had received the tidings through Nathan that he should not build God a house, but that it should be done by his son and successor, he nevertheless did as much towards the carrying out of the desire of his heart as was possible in connection with this declaration of the will of Jahve. He consecrated the site of the future Temple, he procured the necessary means and materials for the building of it, he made all the necessary arrangements for the future Temple-service, he inspirited the people for the gigantic work of building that was before them, and handed over to his son the model for it, as it is all related to us in detail by the chronicler. The divine name “the mighty One of Jacob” is taken from <reference osisRef="Gen.49.24">Gen 49:24</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.24">Isa 1:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.26">Isa 49:26</reference>; Isa 60:16. The Philistines with their Dagon had been made to feel this mighty Rock of Jacob when they took the sacred Ark along with them (<reference osisRef="1Sam.5.1-1Sam.5.12">1Sa 5:1-12</reference>). With אם David solemnly declares what he is resolved not to do. The meaning of the hyperbolically expressed vow in the form of an oath is that for so long he will not rejoice at his own dwelling-house, nor give himself up to sleep that is free from anxiety; in fine, for so long he will not rest. The genitives after אהל and ערשׂ are appositional genitives; Ps 44 delights in similar combinations of synonyms. יצוּעי (Latin <hi type="italic">strata mea</hi>) is a poetical plural, as also is משׁכּנות. With תּנוּמה (which is always said of the eyelids, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.40">Gen 31:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.6.4">Pro 6:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.16">Ecc 8:16</reference>, not of the eyes) alternates שׁנת (according to another reading שׁנת) for שׁנה. The <hi type="italic">āth</hi> is the same as in נחלת in <reference osisRef="Ps.16.6">Psa 16:6</reference>, cf. 60:13, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.2">Exo 15:2</reference>, and frequently. This Aramaizing rejection of the syllable before the tone is, however, without example elsewhere. The lxx adds to <reference osisRef="Ps.132.4">Psa 132:4</reference>, καὶ ἀνάπαυσιν τοῖς κροτάφοις μου (וּמנוּחה לרקּותי), but this is a disagreeable overloading of the verse.
entries.3f3d2aca51396843334458414af78586a9ac7288: <reference osisRef="Ps.132.6-Ps.132.10">Psa 132:6-10</reference> <div eID="gen10227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10228" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.132.6">Psa 132:6</reference> begins the language of the church, which in this Psalm reminds Jahve of His promises and comforts itself with them. Olshausen regards this <reference osisRef="Ps.132.6">Psa 132:6</reference> as altogether inexplicable. The interpretation nevertheless has some safe starting-points. (1) Since the subject spoken of is the founding of a fixed sanctuary, and one worthy of Jahve, the suffix of שׁמענוּה (with <hi type="italic">Chateph</hi> as in Hos 8:2, Ew. §60, <hi type="italic">a</hi>) and מצאנוּה refers to the Ark of the covenant, which is <hi type="italic">fem.</hi> also in other instances (<reference osisRef="1Sam.4.17">1Sa 4:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.11">2Ch 8:11</reference>). (2) The Ark of the covenant, fetched up out of Shiloh by the Israelites to the battle at Ebenezer, fell into the hands of the victors, and remained, having been again given up by them, for twenty years in Kirjath-Jearim (1Sa 7:1.), until David removed it out of this Judaean district to Zion (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.2-2Sam.6.4">2Sa 6:2-4</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.4">2Ch 1:4</reference>). What is then more natural than that שׂדי־יער is a poetical appellation of Kirjath-Jearim (cf. “the field of Zoan” in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.12">Psa 78:12</reference>)? Kirjath-Jearim has, as a general thing, very varying names. It is also called <hi type="italic">Kirjath-ha-jearim</hi> in <reference osisRef="Jer.26.20">Jer 26:20</reference> (<hi type="italic">Kirjath-'arim</hi> in Ezr 2:25, cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.18.28">Jos 18:28</reference>), <hi type="italic">Kirjath-ba'al</hi> in Jos 16:1-10 :50, <hi type="italic">Ba'alah</hi> in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.9">Jos 15:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.6">1Ch 13:6</reference> (cf. <hi type="italic">Har-ha-ba'alah</hi>, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.11">Jos 15:11</reference>, with <hi type="italic">Har-Jearim</hi> in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.10">Jos 15:10</reference>), and, as it seems, even <hi type="italic">Ba'alê Jehudah</hi> in 2Sa 6:2. Why should it not also have been called <hi type="italic">Ja'ar</hi> side by side with <hi type="italic">Kirjath-Jearim</hi>, and more especially if the mountainous district, to which the mention of a hill and mountain of <hi type="italic">Jearim</hi> points, was, as the name “city of the wood” implies, at the same time a wooded district? We therefore fall in with Kühnöl’s (1799) rendering: we found it in the meadows of Jaar, and with his remark: “Jaar is a shortened name of the city of Kirjath-Jearim.” <div eID="gen10228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10229" type="x-p"/> The question now further arises as to what <hi type="italic">Ephrathah</hi> is intended to mean. This is an ancient name of Bethlehem; but the Ark of the covenant never was in Bethlehem. Accordingly Hengstenberg interprets, “We knew of it in Bethlehem (where David had spent his youth) only by hearsay, no one had seen it; we found it in Kirjath-Jearim, yonder in the wooded environs of the city, where it was as it were buried in darkness and solitude.” So even Anton Hulsius (1650): <hi type="italic">Ipse David loquitur, qui dicit illam ipsam arcam, de qua quum adhuc Bethlehemi versaretur inaudivisset, postea a se</hi> (<hi type="italic">vel majroibus suis ipso adhuc minorenni</hi>) <hi type="italic">inventam fuisse in campis Jaar</hi>. But (1) the supposition that David’s words are continued here does not harmonize with the way in which they are introduced in <reference osisRef="Ps.132.2">Psa 132:2</reference>, according to which they cannot possibly extend beyond the vow that follows. (2) If the church is speaking, one does not see why Bethlehem is mentioned in particular as the place of the hearsay. (3) <hi type="italic">We heard it in Ephrathah</hi> cannot well mean anything else than, <hi type="italic">per antiptosin</hi> (as in <reference osisRef="Gen.1.4">Gen 1:4</reference>, but without כּי), we heard that it was in Ephrathah. But the Ark was before Kirjath-Jearim in Shiloh. The former lay in the tribe of Judah close to the western borders of Benjamin, the latter in the midst of the tribe of Ephraim. Now since אפרתי quite as often means an Ephraimite as it does a Bethlehemite, it may be asked whether <hi type="italic">Ephrathah</hi> is not intended of the Ephraimitish territory (Kühnöl, Gesenius, Maurer, Tholuck, and others). The meaning would then be: we had heard that the sacred Ark was in Shiloh, but we found it not there, but in Kirjath-Jearim. And we can easily understand why the poet has mentioned the two places just in this way. <hi type="italic">Ephrāth</hi>, according to its etymon, is fruitful fields, with which are contrasted the fields of the wood - the sacred Ark had fallen from its original, more worthy abode, as it were, into the wilderness. But is it probable, more especially in view of Mic 5:1, that in a connection in which the memory of David is the ruling idea, <hi type="italic">Ephrathah</hi> signifies the land of Ephraim? No, <hi type="italic">Ephrathah</hi> is the name of the district in which Kirjath-Jearim lay. Caleb had, for instance, by Ephrath, his third wife, a son named Hûr (Chûr), <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.19">1Ch 2:19</reference>, This Hûr, the first-born of Ephrathah, is the father of the population of Bethlehem (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.4">1Ch 4:4</reference>), and Shobal, a son of this Hûr, is father of the population of Kirjath-Jearim (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.50">1Ch 2:50</reference>). Kirjath-Jearim is therefore, so to speak, the daughter of Bethlehem. This was called Ephrathah in ancient times, and this name of Bethlehem became the name of its district (Mic 5:1). Kirjath-Jearim belonged to <hi type="italic">Caleb-Ephrathah </hi>(<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.24">1Ch 2:24</reference>), as the northern part of this district seems to have been called in distinction from <hi type="italic">Negeb-Caleb</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.30.14">1Sa 30:14</reference>). <div eID="gen10229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10230" type="x-p"/> But משׁכּנותיו in <reference osisRef="Ps.132.7">Psa 132:7</reference> is now neither a designation of the house of Abinadab in Kirjath-Jearim, for the expression would be too grand, and in relation to <reference osisRef="Ps.132.5">Psa 132:5</reference> even confusing, nor a designation of the Salomonic Temple-building, for the expression standing thus by itself is not enough alone to designate it. What is meant will therefore be the tent-temple erected by David for the Ark when removed to Zion (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.2">2Sa 7:2</reference>, יריעה). The church arouses itself to enter this, and to prostrate itself in adoration towards (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.99.5">Psa 99:5</reference>) the footstool of Jahve, i.e., the Ark; and to what purpose? The ark of the covenant is now to have a place more worthy of it; the מנוּחה, i.e., the בּית מנוּחה,    <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.2">1Ch 28:2</reference>, in which David’s endeavours have through Solomon reached their goal, is erected: let Jahve and the Ark of His sovereign power, that may not be touched (see the examples of its inviolable character in 1Sa 5:1-12, 1 Sam 6, 2Sa 6:6.), now enter this fixed abode! Let His priests who are to serve Him there clothe themselves in “righteousness,” i.e., in conduct that is according to His will and pleasure; let His saints, who shall there seek and find mercy, shout for joy! More especially, however, let Jahve for David’s sake, His servant, to whose restless longing this place of rest owes its origin, not turn back the face of His anointed one, i.e., not reject his face which there turns towards Him in the attitude of prayer (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.84.10">Psa 84:10</reference>). The chronicler has understood <reference osisRef="Ps.132.10">Psa 132:10</reference> as an intercession on behalf of Solomon, and the situation into which we are introduced by <reference osisRef="Ps.132.6-Ps.132.8">Psa 132:6-8</reference> seems to require this. It is, however, possible that a more recent poet here, in <reference osisRef="Ps.132.7-Ps.132.8">Psa 132:7-8</reference>, reproduces words taken from the heart of the church in Solomon’s time, and blends petitions of the church of the present with them. The subject all through is the church, which is ever identical although changing in the persons of its members. The Israel that brought the sacred Ark out of Kirjath-Jearim to Zion and accompanied it thence to the Temple-hill, and now worships in the sanctuary raised by David’s zeal for the glory of Jahve, is one and the same. The prayer for the priests, for all the saints, and more especially for the reigning king, that then resounded at the dedication of the Temple, is continued so long as the history of Israel lasts, even in a time when Israel has no king, but has all the stronger longing for the fulfilment of the Messianic promise.
entries.c1e27e102465f9f4d20371be6fa3a0ed94ad17d2: <reference osisRef="Ps.132.11-Ps.132.13">Psa 132:11-13</reference> <div eID="gen10230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10231" type="x-p"/> The “for the sake of David” is here set forth in detail. אמת in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.132.11">Psa 132:11</reference></hi> is not the accusative of the object, but an adverbial accusative. The first member of the verse closes with לדוד, which has the distinctive <hi type="italic">Pazer</hi>, which is preceded by <hi type="italic">Legarmeh</hi> as a sub-distinctive; then follows at the head of the second member אמת with <hi type="italic">Zinnor</hi>, then לא־ישׁוּב ממּנּה with <hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi> and its conjunctive <hi type="italic">Galgal</hi>, which regularly precedes after the sub-distinctive <hi type="italic">Zinnor</hi>. The suffix of ממּנּה refers to that which was affirmed by oath, as in Jer 4:28. Lineal descendants of David will Jahve place on the throne (לכסּא like לראשׁי in <reference osisRef="Ps.21.4">Psa 21:4</reference>) to him, i.e., so that they shall follow his as possessors of the throne. David’s children shall for ever (which has been finally fulfilled in Christ) sit לכסּא to him (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.9.5">Jer 9:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.36.7">Jer 36:7</reference>). Thus has Jahve promised, and expects in return from the sons of David the observance of His Law. Instead of עדתי זוּ it is pointed עדתי זו. In Hahn’s edition עדתי has <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> in the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>. (cf. the retreat of the tone in זה אדני, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.17">Dan 10:17</reference>), and in Baer’s edition the still better attested reading <hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi> instead of the counter-tone <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>. It is not plural with a singular suffix (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.28.59">Deu 28:59</reference>, Ges. §91, 3), but, as זו = זאת indicates, the singular for עדוּתי, like תּחנתי for תּחנוּתי in 2Ki 6:8; and signifies the revelation of God as an attestation of His will. אלמּדם has <hi type="italic">Mercha mahpach</hi>., זו <hi type="italic">Rebia parvum</hi>, and עדתי <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi>; and according to the interpunction it would have to be rendered: “and My self-attestation there” (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.9.16">Psa 9:16</reference>), but zow is relative: My self-attestation (revelation), which I teach them. The divine words extend to the end of Psa 132:12. The hypotheses with אם, as the fulfilment in history shows, were conditions of the continuity of the Davidic succession; not, however - because human unfaithfulness does not annul the faithfulness of God - of the endlessness of the Davidic throne. In <reference osisRef="Ps.132.13">Psa 132:13</reference> the poet states the ground of such promissory mercy. It is based on the universal mercy of the election of Jerusalem. אוּהּ has <hi type="italic">He mappic</hi>. like ענּה in <reference osisRef="Deut.22.29">Deu 22:29</reference>, or the stroke of <hi type="italic">Raphe</hi> (Ew. §247, <hi type="italic">d</hi>), although the suffix is not absolutely necessary. In the following strophe the purport of the election of Jerusalem is also unfolded in Jahve’s own words.
entries.39be4f31facec5b697b569f3d2947b1564fd114e: <reference osisRef="Ps.132.14-Ps.132.18">Psa 132:14-18</reference> <div eID="gen10231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10232" type="x-p"/> Shiloh has been rejected (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.60">Psa 78:60</reference>), for a time only was the sacred Ark in Bethel (Jdg 20:27) and Mizpah (Jdg 21:5), only somewhat over twenty years was it sheltered by the house of Abinadab in Kirjath-Jearim (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.2">1Sa 7:2</reference>), only three months by the house of Obed-Edom in Perez-uzzah (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.11">2Sa 6:11</reference>) - but Zion is Jahve’s abiding dwelling-place, His own proper settlement, מנוּחה (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">Isa 11:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.1">Isa 66:1</reference>, and besides <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.2">1Ch 28:2</reference>). In Zion, His chosen and beloved dwelling-place, Jahve blesses everything that belongs to her temporal need (צידהּ for זידתהּ, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Psa 27:5</reference>, note); so that her poor do not suffer want, for divine love loves the poor most especially. His second blessing refers to the priests, for by means of these He will keep up His intercourse with His people. He makes the priesthood of Zion a real institution of salvation: He clothes her priests with salvation, so that they do not merely bring it about instrumentally, but personally possess it, and their whole outward appearance is one which proclaims salvation. And to all her saints He gives cause and matter for high and lasting joy, by making Himself known also to the church, in which He has taken up His abode, in deeds of mercy (loving-kindness or grace). There (שׁם, <reference osisRef="Ps.133.3">Psa 133:3</reference>) in Zion is indeed the kingship of promise, which cannot fail of fulfilment. He will cause a horn to shoot forth, He will prepare a lamp, for the house of David, which David here represents as being its ancestor and the anointed one of God reigning at that time; and all who hostilely rise up against David in his seed, He will cover with shame as with a garment (<reference osisRef="Job.8.22">Job 8:22</reference>), and the crown consecrated by promise, which the seed of David wears, shall blossom like an unfading wreath. The horn is an emblem of defensive might and victorious dominion, and the lamp (נר,    <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.17">2Sa 21:17</reference>, cf. ניר, <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.7">2Ch 21:7</reference>, lxx λύχνον) an emblem of brilliant dignity and joyfulness. In view of <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.21">Eze 29:21</reference>, of the predictions concerning the Branch (<hi type="italic">zemach</hi>) in <reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">Isa 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jer 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.15">Jer 33:15</reference>; Zec 3:8; Zec 6:12 (cf. <reference osisRef="Heb.7.14">Heb 7:14</reference>), and of the fifteenth Beracha of the <hi type="italic">Shemone - Esre</hi> (the daily Jewish prayer consisting of eighteen benedictions): “make the branch (<hi type="italic">zemach</hi>) of David Thy servant to shoot forth speedily, and let his horn rise high by virtue of Thy salvation,” - it is hardly to be doubted that the poet attached a Messianic meaning to this promise. With reference to our Psalm, Zacharias, the father of John the Baptist, changes that supplicatory beracha of his nation (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.68-Luke.1.70">Luk 1:68-70</reference>) into a praiseful one, joyfully anticipating the fulfilment that is at hand in Jesus.  <chapter eID="Ps.132"/> <div eID="gen10232" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 132
The writer of this Psalm, whoever he may have been
Lightfoot ascribes this Psalm to David, and supposes it to have been composed on the second removal of the Ark from the house of Obededom. (1 Chronicles 15:4, etc.) But the mention of David’s name in the tenth verse in the third person, and the terms there employed, militate against his being the Author. Others ascribe it to Solomon, who, they think, wrote it about the time of the removing of the Ark into the Temple, which he had built for it. (2 Chronicles 5:2, etc.) Others are of opinion, that it was composed by Solomon for the solemn services that were celebrated at the dedication of the Temple. “The whole tenor of this Psalm,” says Jebb, “is an exact epitome of the Dedication Prayer of Solomon. (2 Chronicles 6) The topics are the same ­ the building the house of the Lord ­ the promise to David ­ the inhabitation of the Almighty; ­ and the concluding sentences of the Dedication, are identical with those expressions of the Psalm in verses 8, 9, 10. There can, therefore, be little question that this Psalm was composed by Solomon.” ­ Jebb’s Literal Translation of the Book of Psalms, etc., volume 2. As this forms one of the “Songs of Degrees,” those who conceive that these Psalms were so called beta. use sung by the Jews about the time of their return from Babylon, conclude that Ezra selected this ancient song to be sung at the dedication of the second Temple.
here, in the name of all the faithful, puts God in remembrance of his promise, that he would never suffer his house or kingdom to fail, but support and defend both.

The expression of going up to one’s bed may be illustrated by what Dr. Shaw says of the Moorish houses in Barbary. Having observed that their chambers are spacious, of the same length with the square court, in the sides of which they are built, he adds, “At one end of each chamber there is a little gallery raised three, four, or five feet above the floor, with a balustrade in the front of it, with a few steps likewise leading up to it. Here they place their beds; a situation frequently alluded to in the Holy Scriptures.” The language of the text is no doubt hyperbolical, as Calvin observes, being intended to express David’s great anxiety to have a house built for the worship of God.
4. If I give sleep to mine eyes, slumber to mine eyelids, 5. Until I, find a place for Jehovah, habitations

for the Mighty One of Jacob ­
אביר יעקבabir Yaaicob, the Mighty One of Jacob. By this expression, which occurs both here and in Psalm 132:2, the Psalmist evidently has a reference to the Patriarch’s own words which he employed in his blessing to Joseph, where God is emphatically so designated. (Genesis 49:24.) From this Hebrew name אביר, abir, and כביר, cabir, which is synonymous, probably came the Cabiri, or the great gods of the Grecians, and the Abiry of the Druids. See Thes. Antiq. Roman. tom. 5 page 760; Bryant’s Myth. volume 2: page 473; and Cooke’s Patriarchal and Druidical Religion.
 
1. O Jehovah! remember David. Interpreters are not agreed respecting the penman of this Psalm, though there is little doubt that it was either David or Solomon. At the solemn dedication of the Temple, when Solomon prayed, several verses are mentioned in the sacred history as having been quoted by him, from which we may infer that the Psalm was sufficiently well known to the people, or that Solomon applied a few words of it for an occasion in reference to which he had written the whole Psalm. The name of David is prominently mentioned, because it was to him that the continuance of the kingdom and Temple was promised, and though dead, this could not affect the truthfulness of God’s word. The Church could very properly pray in the manner which is here done, that God would perform what he had promised to his servant David, not as a private individual, but in favor of all his people. It was therefore a preposterous idea of the Papists to argue from this passage that we may be benefitted by the intercession of the dead. Just as if the faithful were here to be understood as calling up an advocate from the tomb to plead their cause with God, when it is abundantly evident from the context that they look entirely to the covenant which God had made with David, knowing well that though given to one man, it was with the understanding that it should be communicated to all. There is a propriety why mention should be made of his affliction or humiliation. Some render the word meekness, but there is no reason for this whatsoever. In 2 Chronicles 6:42, it is true we read of חסדים; that is, mercies, which I consider to be there understood in the passive sense, as meaning the benefits which had been conferred upon David; but I am clearly of opinion that here the reference is to the anxious cares, the numerous difficulties and struggles which David had to undergo, so long as he was kept by God in suspense. Remember, as if it had been said, the great anxieties, the heavy troubles, which David endured before he came to the kingdom, and how fervently and earnestly he desired to build the Temple, though he was not allowed to do it during his whole life. The dangers, labors, and troubles which he underwent, must clearly have confirmed the faith of God’s people in the truth of the divine oracle, inasmuch as they showed how firmly and certainly he was himself convinced of the truth of what God had spoken. Some insert the copulative reading, remember David and affliction; but of this I do not approve. The particle את eth, rather denotes that special respect in which they would have David remembered, viz., as regarded his afflictions, or that he might come forth before the view of God with his afflictions, and obtain his desire according to them.

                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:511" />7 We will go <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Seeing the Ark is now fixed in a certain place, we will go to it more generally and constantly than formerly we did.</ns0:note> into his tabernacles <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Into his Tabernacle or Temple, the Plural number put for the Singular, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 43. 3. & 46. 4, &c.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 99. 5.</ns0:note> we will worship at his footstool <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Either the Temple: or rather the Ark, so called 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 28. 2. <ns0:hi>La<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment.</ns0:hi> 2. 1. because God is oft said to <ns0:hi>sit between the Cheru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bims,</ns0:hi> which were above the Ark.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
